=== Forgiveness and revenge ===

Topic: Forgiveness and revenge (forgiveness_and_revenge) — forced by request

--- Christianity — obligatory ---

  • The Lord's Prayer binds divine forgiveness to our forgiving, making it a requirement of the praying life. [C1]
      “For if ye forgive men their trespasses, your heavenly Father will also forgive you: But if ye forgive not men their trespasses, neither will your Father forgive your trespasses.”

      “Dearly beloved, avenge not yourselves, but rather give place unto wrath: for it is written, Vengeance is mine; I will repay, saith the Lord.”
      — Romans 12:19 — The Holy Bible, King James Version, trans. the King James translators (1611)

  Further reading:

--- Islam — encouraged ---

Justice is the floor; forgiveness is the summons.
  • Like-for-like response is bounded and pardon joined to amendment is rewarded by God. [C3]
      “The guerdon of an ill-deed is an ill the like thereof. But whosoever pardoneth and amendeth, his wage is the affair of Allah. Lo! He loveth not wrong-doers.”
      — Qur'an 42:40 — The Meaning of the Glorious Koran, trans. Marmaduke Pickthall (1930)

  • Answering evil with something better transforms enmity itself. [C4]
      “The good deed and the evil deed are not alike. Repel the evil deed with one which is better, then lo! he, between whom and thee there was enmity (will become) as though he was a bosom friend.”

--- Judaism — context_dependent ---

  • Leviticus forbids revenge and grudge-bearing in the verse that commands neighbor-love. [C5]

      - Louis E. Newman, “Repentance: The Meaning and Practice of Teshuvah” (2010) [book]

--- Buddhism — obligatory ---
Hatred never ceases by hatred — this is presented not as commandment but as observed law, like fire needing fuel. Resentment held is suffering self-inflicted; the practice is to meet anger with love and the greedy with liberality, dissolving the enmity rather than repaying it. Forgiveness here is less a favor to the offender than the release of one's own burning.
  • The old rule: hatred ceases only by love, so revenge merely continues the harm into oneself. [C7]
      “For hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love, this is an old rule.”
      — Dhp 5 — The Dhammapada, trans. F. Max Müller (1881)

      “Let a man overcome anger by love, let him overcome evil by good; let him overcome the greedy by liberality, the liar by truth!”
      — Dhp 223 — The Dhammapada, trans. F. Max Müller (1881)
      Context: Each vice is met by its counter-virtue: the practical method behind the teaching that hatred cannot end hatred.

      - Sharon Salzberg, “Lovingkindness: The Revolutionary Art of Happiness” (1995) [book]

--- Stoicism — reframed ---
The Stoic does not exactly forgive — he declines to be injured. Wrongdoers act from ignorance of good and evil and remain kin; no one can fix ugliness on you but yourself, so there is nothing to avenge. The best revenge is not to become like the wrong-doer. What other traditions frame as pardoning an injury, Stoicism reframes as correcting the judgment that an injury occurred.
  • The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong-doer. [C9]
      “The best way of avenging thyself is not to become like the wrong-doer.”
      — Meditations VI.6 — The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, trans. George Long (1862)
      Context: Marcus's one-line answer to revenge: the only injury the wrongdoer can really do you is to make you resemble him.
  • The morning rehearsal: offenders act from ignorance, remain kin, and cannot injure the ruling faculty. [C10]
      “Begin the morning by saying to thyself, I shall meet with the busy-body, the ungrateful, arrogant, deceitful, envious, unsocial. All these things happen to them by reason of their ignorance of what is good and evil.”
      — Meditations II.1 — The Meditations of Marcus Aurelius, trans. George Long (1862)
      Context: The opening of the emperor's morning rehearsal; the passage continues by arguing that the wrongdoer is kin and that we are made for co-operation, so neither anger nor hatred fits.
  Further reading:
      - Martha C. Nussbaum, “Anger and Forgiveness: Resentment, Generosity, Justice” (2016) [book]

--- Virtue ethics — context_dependent ---

Past that point the question turns on what the injured party's own temper is doing. Nursing a grievance is listed among the faults: sullen people hold their resentment because they cannot discharge it, and retaliation feels like resolution because it swaps pain for pleasure. Yet the opposite counsel is refused too, since someone who never resents an injury done to those he loves has failed them.
  • Pardon is the fitting response to involuntary wrongdoing, and it is established before any question of generosity arises. [C11]
      “Since virtue is concerned with passions and actions, and on voluntary passions and actions praise and blame are bestowed, on those that are involuntary pardon, and sometimes also pity, to distinguish the voluntary and the involuntary is presumably necessary for those who are studying the nature of virtue.”
      — NE III.1, 1109b30 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: The opening of Book III, which makes voluntariness the gatekeeper of praise and blame. Pardon here is not a gift bestowed on the guilty but the correct response to an act that was not fully the agent's own.
  • The sullen grudge is classified as a vice of excess, and revenge is described as its relief rather than its cure. [C12]
      “Sulky people are hard to appease, and retain their anger long; for they repress their passion. But it ceases when they retaliate; for revenge relieves them of their anger, producing in them pleasure instead of pain.”
      — NE IV.5, 1126a20 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: A clinical description of the grudge, listed among the vices of excess. Aristotle explains why revenge feels like resolution while naming the state it resolves as a defect of character.
  • Corrective punishment by proper authority counts as a part of justice, and is distinguished from private hatred by what it aims at. [C13]
      “Vengeance is lawful and virtuous so far as it tends to the prevention of evil.”
      — ST II-II, Q.108, art.1 — Summa Theologica, trans. Fathers of the English Dominican Province (1920)
      Context: Aquinas treats vindicatio as a potential part of justice, distinguishing corrective punishment aimed at restraining wrongdoing from private hatred. The permission is tightly conditioned on right authority and right intention.
  • Absorbing insult to one's friends without protest is named a servile defect, not patience. [C14]
      “For such a man is thought not to feel things nor to be pained by them, and, since he does not get angry, he is thought unlikely to defend himself; and to endure being insulted and put up with insult to one's friends is slavish.”
      — NE IV.5, 1126a7 — The Nicomachean Ethics, trans. W. D. Ross (1925)
      Context: Aristotle's hardest line against unconditional patience. He is describing a failure of self-respect and of loyalty, not recommending retaliation, and the following lines still condemn excess.
  Note: There is no ancient Greek term that maps onto unconditional forgiveness, and scholars disagree whether that is a gap in the psychology or a considered refusal. The scholastic reworking adds mercy as a virtue while keeping corrective vengeance inside justice, which leaves the tension in place rather than dissolving it.

      - David Konstan, “Before Forgiveness: The Origins of a Moral Idea” (2010) [book]
